lede: Dead leaves, wood and bodies do not simply vanish: fungi and bacteria break them down and release the nutrients locked inside. That step is one arrow on the carbon cycle, the loop that moves carbon between the air, plants, animals and the ground.
can: Describe saprophytic feeding as secretion, extracellular digestion and absorption.
Name the conditions that speed up decay and calculate a rate.
Say which carbon-cycle processes add carbon dioxide and which one removes it.

md: Leave an apple core in the garden and in a few weeks it is gone. Fungi and bacteria took it apart, and the carbon in it went back into the air and the soil.

md:
A **saprophyte** is an organism that feeds on **dead** material. Saprophytic **fungi and bacteria** do it in three steps, and every step is a marking point.

**1 Secretion.** The fungus or bacterium **secretes enzymes out of its cells** onto the dead material.
**2 Extracellular digestion.** The enzymes **break the large insoluble molecules down outside the cell** — that is exactly what *extracellular* means.
**3 Absorption.** The small **soluble products** are then **absorbed** back into the cells.

prompt: Digestion by a fungus happens outside its cells, so it is called ______ digestion.
explain: Extracellular: extra- meaning outside, cellular meaning of the cell. It is the word the scheme lists, and it earns its own mark.

title: Why outside, and why it matters to everything else
md: Large molecules such as starch and protein are far too big to cross a cell membrane, and a fungus has no mouth to take them in first. So it turns the problem inside out: send the enzymes to the food instead of bringing the food to the enzymes. What this does for the ecosystem is **recycle nutrients** — carbon, nitrogen and minerals locked up in dead leaves, wood and bodies are released back into the soil where plants can take them up again — and it builds **humus**, the dark, crumbly organic material in soil.

prompt: Why must a fungus digest its food outside its cells?
options: the molecules are too large to cross the cell membrane
it has no enzymes inside its cells
the soil is too cold inside the cell
answer: the molecules are too large to cross the cell membrane
explain: Large molecules cannot cross the membrane, so the enzymes go out to the food instead.

md: Decomposers are living things, so they decay material fastest when the conditions suit **them**: **warm** (their enzymes work faster, but not so hot that the enzymes are denatured), **moist** (they need water, and enzymes work in solution) and **aerobic** (they respire aerobically, which releases far more energy than anaerobic respiration). Bag **A**, warm and moist with plenty of air, lost **48 g** of its **60 g** in 12 weeks. Bag **C**, warm but waterlogged so the air was excluded, lost only **12 g**. Waterlogging is why peat bogs preserve wood and leaves for thousands of years.

prompt: Which set of conditions gives the fastest decay?
options: warm, moist and plenty of air
cold, moist and plenty of air
answer: warm, moist and plenty of air
explain: All three at once. Take away the warmth, the water or the air and the decomposers slow right down.

prompt: Bag C fell from 60 g to 48 g over 12 weeks. What was the rate of decomposition, in grams per week?
explain: (60 − 48) ÷ 12 = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 g per week. Divide by the whole time the experiment ran, not by the gap between two readings — March 2026 examiners said many candidates divided by an incorrect time.

md: Only **one** process removes carbon dioxide from the air: **photosynthesis**. Three put it back: **respiration, combustion, decomposition**. The rest move carbon **between organisms** without touching the air at all — **feeding** passes it along a chain, **excretion** and **egestion** pass it to dead material, and **fossilisation** locks it away underground for millions of years until combustion releases it.

prompt: Which process moves carbon from a dead animal into the soil?
explain: Decomposition. Fossilisation locks carbon underground instead, and photosynthesis takes it from the air.

title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q2(b) — respiration in both columns
md: The question gave a two-column table: processes that **add** carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, and processes that **remove** it. **Many candidates put respiration in both columns.** Respiration only ever produces carbon dioxide — in a plant just as much as in an animal. The reason a plant takes carbon dioxide in during the day is photosynthesis happening faster than respiration, not respiration running backwards.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Carbon Cycle"
why: The whole cycle drawn arrow by arrow in a few minutes. Watch it, then answer the question underneath without looking back at the diagram.

prompt: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
explain: Photosynthesis, and only photosynthesis. The other three all release carbon dioxide back into the air.

title: PhET: Greenhouse Effect
attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
task: Open the Waves or Layer Model screen and move the carbon dioxide concentration from its ice-age setting to its present-day setting. Then write two sentences: name the carbon-cycle process that has raised the concentration since 1750, and name the one process that removes carbon dioxide again. (The physics of how the gas traps heat belongs to a different unit — here you are only using the simulation to see the size of the change.)

prompt: Dead plants buried under mud and turned into coal over millions of years is the process called ______.
explain: Fossilisation. It is the slowest arrow on the cycle, and combustion is what brings that carbon back in a single afternoon.

md:
Describe decomposition as **secrete enzymes, digest outside the cell, absorb**.
Name the conditions for fast decay: **warm, moist, aerobic**.
Calculate a **rate of decomposition**.
Name the one process that **removes** carbon dioxide from the air.
Place **respiration, combustion** and **fossilisation** on the cycle.

Two shapes recur: a carbon-cycle diagram with lettered boxes and a two-column sorting table, or a decay investigation with a results table, a trend and an explanation. The listing rule bites on the sorting table — a right answer beside a wrong one in the same column earns nothing. Stuck: name the process for each arrow you can read.
